newsitem.title: HONG KONG: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - JG Summit tops day's deals.
newsitem.headline: ASIAN DEBT MARKETS - JG Summit tops day's deals.

text.p: Philippines corporate JG Summit was the top of the news in Asian debt markets on Tuesday.
The company's long-awaited US$200 million Eurobond launched in London via lead manager ING Barings.
The bond, with pay date November 96 and maturity May 2002, will be priced to yield 180 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. Fees are 62.5 basis points.
Bankers were generally positive on the bond.
"I think it should go fine. The timing certainly is right," said a syndicate manager in Hong Kong. "JG Summit is the largest conglomerate in the Philippines and is very well known."
The company has interests in cement, petrochemicals, food, telecommunications, banking and property. It is majority owned by the family of Chinese-Filipino tycoon John Gokongwei Jr.
Listed companies under JG Summit include Philippine Commercial International Bank, which launched a five-year US$100 million bond in September through Merrill Lynch.
Lead manager ING Barings spent weeks presenting the deal to investors in the U.S., Europe and Asia.

"This was not a deal that was created and done. We roadshowed it for over three and half weeks with the idea of continuing the trend of building the fixed rate market for Asian borrowers," said ING Barings head of syndicate Manuel Carrelet, who is based in London.
Because JG Summit is a conglomerate and a fast-growing company, it is difficult to analyze and investors wanted time to study the credit carefully, he said.

Carrelet said ING Barings kept more than 80 percent of the transaction. More than 35 percent of its allocation went to the U.S., just under 50 percent ended up in Asia and the remainder was taken up by accounts in the rest of the world, he said.
Syndicate managers in Asia said the 180 spread plus fees made sense given the current market for Philippine corporate credits, which is booming.

For example, Ayala Corp paper due November 2001 is trading in the secondary market in the mid-150s over Treasuries. It was priced to yield 173 basis points over the benchmark when it launched in May. Fees were 75 basis points.
SM Prime's bond due February 2002 priced at 200 basis points over Treasuries while fees totalled 75 basis points. That bond now is trading at 180-190 over Treasuries.
"It makes sense to price JG Summit somewhere in between Ayala and SM Prime," remarked one source.

Some bankers complained about the syndication style, charging ING Barings permitted syndicate managers to sign on for only small amounts with the stipulation that they take far more at the re-offer level. Carrelet brushed off the criticism.
"If I am sold out, I can't increase the size of the syndicate," he said.
Also from the Philippines, Allied Bank launched a US$50 million floating rate certificate of deposit issue through arranger Standard Chartered Investment Banking.
The three-year paper pays a margin of 85 basis points over the three-month London Interbank Offered Rate and an all-in return of 92 basis points.
Like other Philippine banks, Allied is paying a lot less for this FRCD than for a similar deal launched earlier this year. That deal offered an all-in of 112 basis points for three years.

Elsewhere, Schroders Asia is tipped to have won the mandate for a HKS$600 million FRCD issue for Shanghai Commercial Bank. The deal is expected to have a five-year final maturity, puts and calls in year three and an all-in return of 43 basis points.
Schroders declined to comment on the deal.
At HK$600 million, the Shanghai Commercial Bank deal would not be eligible for the Hong Kong Monetary Authority's Liquidity Adjustment Facility, or discount window.
Bankers said Dao Heng Bank and Dah Sing Bank still are taking bids on LAF-eligible borrowings.
